Let

\[
S=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\sum_{j=1}^{100}2^{-\left\lfloor 101k/j\right\rfloor}.
\]

Group the terms by the value of the floor. For \(n\ge 1\), let

\[
N_n=\#\{(j,k):1\le j\le 100,\ k\ge 1,\ \lfloor 101k/j\rfloor=n\}.
\]

Then

\[
S=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} N_n 2^{-n}.
\]

For fixed \(n\) and \(j\),

\[
\left\lfloor \frac{101k}{j}\right\rfloor=n
\iff
nj\le 101k<(n+1)j.
\]

Write \(nj=101q+r\) with \(0\le r<101\). Since \(j<101\), the interval \([nj,(n+1)j)\) has length less than \(101\), so it contains at most one multiple of \(101\). It contains one exactly when either

- \(r=0\), so the left endpoint is a multiple of \(101\), or
- \(r+j>101\), so the next multiple of \(101\) lies inside the interval.

Thus

\[
N_n=\#\{j\in\{1,\dots,100\}: r=0 \text{ or } r+j>101\},
\]

where \(r\equiv nj\pmod{101}\).

Because \(101\) is prime and \(1\le j\le 100\), \(r=0\) occurs for every \(j\) iff \(101\mid n\). In that case,

\[
N_n=100.
\]

Otherwise, let \(t\equiv n\pmod{101}\) with \(1\le t\le 100\). Then \(r\) is the least positive residue of \(tj\pmod{101}\).

- If \(t=100\), then \(r\equiv -j\pmod{101}\), so \(r=101-j\) and \(r+j=101\) for every \(j\). Hence \(N_n=0\).
- If \(1\le t\le 99\), consider the \(100\) pairs \((j,r)\) satisfying \(r\equiv tj\pmod{101}\). The map

\[
(j,r)\mapsto (101-j,101-r)
\]

is a fixed-point-free involution preserving this set. No pair has \(j+r=101\), because that would imply \((t+1)j\equiv 0\pmod{101}\), impossible for \(1\le t\le 99\). Therefore the involution pairs the \(50\) pairs with \(j+r<101\) with the \(50\) pairs with \(j+r>101\). Hence

\[
N_n=50.
\]

So \(N_n\) is \(101\)-periodic, and in one period

\[
N_1=\cdots=N_{99}=50,\qquad N_{100}=0,\qquad N_{101}=100.
\]

Therefore

\[
S=\frac{50\sum_{n=1}^{99}2^{-n}+100\cdot 2^{-101}}{1-2^{-101}}.
\]

Now

\[
50\sum_{n=1}^{99}2^{-n}+100\cdot 2^{-101}
=50(1-2^{-99})+100\cdot 2^{-101}
=50(1-2^{-100}).
\]

Thus

\[
S=\frac{50(1-2^{-100})}{1-2^{-101}}
=\frac{100(2^{100}-1)}{2^{101}-1}.
\]

\[
\boxed{\frac{100(2^{100}-1)}{2^{101}-1}}
\]
